blocks.prompt: A Nose With No Bones
blocks.text: An elephant's trunk is its nose and its top lip, joined together. There is not one bone inside it. It bends any way the elephant wants. A trunk can lift a heavy log. It can also pick up one small seed. When an elephant is thirsty, it sucks water up into its trunk. Then it curls the trunk into its mouth and lets the water go. An elephant does not drink through its trunk like a straw. It uses the trunk like a bucket.

notes: African elephants have the biggest ears of any animal
Elephants barely sweat
Ears work like a radiator
They rumble too low for people to hear

blocks.prompt: Big Ears Are for Hearing and for Cooling Down
blocks.text: An elephant lives in hot places, and a big body is hard to cool down. Sweat is not the answer. Elephants barely sweat at all. Their ears are the answer. Each big ear is packed with blood vessels that run close to the surface of the skin. When an elephant flaps its ears, moving air cools the blood inside them. That cooled blood travels back through the body. African elephants live in the hottest, most open country, and they have the largest ears of any animal on Earth. Ears do something else too. Elephants talk to each other in deep rumbles, so low that human ears cannot hear them. These rumbles roll across the ground for miles. An elephant can pick them up through its feet, feeling the faint shaking in the soil. So a herd can be spread far apart and still stay together. Two elephants may seem silent to you. They are having a conversation you cannot hear.

blocks.prompt: Answer each question in a full sentence.

answers: elephants barely sweat at all
moving air cools the blood in the vessels near the skin, and that cooled blood travels back through the body
it feels the faint shaking in the soil
(inference: they live in the hottest, most open country, so they need more cooling)

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Eats about 300 pounds of plants a day
Only four working molars at a time
Each molar is about the size of a brick
New teeth slide in from the back, not from below
Six sets in a lifetime, and no seventh
The last set arrives at about age thirty

blocks.prompt: Elephant Teeth Are on a Conveyor Belt
blocks.text: An elephant spends about sixteen hours of every day eating. It has to. It pushes roughly three hundred pounds of grass, bark, roots, and branches through its body daily, and much of that food is tough, dry, and full of grit. All that chewing wears teeth down fast. Your teeth would not survive it. Neither would a horse's. So elephants solved the problem in a way no other animal quite matches. An elephant does not have a mouth full of teeth. It has four working molars, one in each corner, and each one is about the size of a brick. When those molars wear flat, the elephant does not lose them downward the way your baby teeth fell out. New molars push in from the back of the jaw and slide forward, shoving the worn ones ahead of them until the old stubs crumble away at the front. It works like a conveyor belt. An elephant gets six sets in a lifetime. The sixth set arrives when the elephant is around thirty years old, and it is the last one. There is no seventh. When those final molars wear smooth, usually somewhere past sixty, the elephant can no longer grind its food. It grows thin even while standing in deep grass. For most wild elephants, this is how life ends. Not a predator, not a disease. A worn-out tooth. Old elephants often move to soft marsh plants near water for their last months, which is one reason people once believed in elephant graveyards.

answers: new molars push in from the back and shove the worn ones forward until they crumble away at the front
baby teeth fall out downward, but elephant molars are pushed forward from the back of the jaw
(inference: its last molars are worn smooth, so it cannot grind food even when food is all around it)
(inference: old elephants gather near water to eat soft plants, so their bones ended up in the same places)

notes: A herd is led by a matriarch, usually the oldest female
Elephants can live sixty to seventy years
Rumbles carry for miles through the ground
Older matriarchs tell male lions from female by sound
Poachers target the biggest tusks, which means the oldest animals

blocks.prompt: The Oldest Female Knows the Way
blocks.text: In 1993 a drought settled over Tarangire, in northern Tanzania, and did not lift. Grass failed. Waterholes shrank to cracked mud. Calves began to die, and researchers found that the losses were not spread evenly. Some family groups lost almost no young. One lost far more. The difference came down to the age of the female in front. An elephant herd is a line of related females and their young, led by a matriarch, usually the oldest among them. She does not rule by strength. She rules by memory. She has walked this land for fifty or sixty years, and she carries a map no one else has: where water still runs in a bad year, which route crosses the driest ground, which valley held food the last time the rains failed. During that drought, two groups walked out of the park entirely, to places their families had not used in decades. Their matriarchs were old enough to have lived through the last great drought, more than thirty years earlier. The group that stayed behind had a younger matriarch. It lost the most calves. Her memory does other work as well. Play a recording of lions roaring to a herd, and the response depends on who is listening. Younger matriarchs often bunch up nervously at any roar. Older ones listen more carefully. They can tell three lions from one, and male lions from female, and they mount a defense only when the threat is real. Male lions are far more dangerous to a calf, and the older matriarchs know it. This is why losing old elephants costs more than losing one animal. Ivory poachers target the biggest tusks, and the biggest tusks belong to the oldest elephants. When a matriarch is shot, the herd does not simply lose a member. It loses the map. It loses the judgment. A young female inherits a family she does not yet know how to lead, through country she has only half learned, and her mistakes will show up years later as calves that did not survive a dry season. The knowledge took sixty years to build. It can be erased in an afternoon.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A tusk is an upper incisor that never stops growing
Mozambique civil war: 1977 to 1992
Gorongosa lost about 90 percent of its elephants
Tuskless females went from about 1 in 5 to about half
The trait appears X-linked, dominant, and lethal in males
Candidate gene AMELX helps build tooth enamel

blocks.prompt: The Elephants That Stopped Growing Tusks
blocks.text: A tusk is not a horn. It is a tooth, an upper incisor that never stopped growing, pushing forward out of the skull for the whole of an elephant's life. An elephant uses it the way you might use a crowbar and a shovel and a set of car keys: stripping bark from trees, levering apart roots, digging into dry riverbeds for water buried under the sand, sparring with rivals, resting a heavy trunk. Tusks are useful. Tusks are also ivory, and that is the problem. Between 1977 and 1992, Mozambique fought a civil war. Both sides needed money, and Gorongosa National Park was full of it, walking around on four legs. Fighters shot elephants and traded the ivory for weapons and supplies. By the end of the war the park's elephant population had fallen by about ninety percent. A few hundred animals were left where thousands had been. Then researchers noticed something strange about the survivors. Roughly half of the adult females had no tusks at all. Tusklessness was not new. Before the war, somewhere around one in five Gorongosa females was born without tusks, a natural variation, mostly harmless. What changed was the selection pressure. A hunter looking for ivory walks past an elephant that has none. In ordinary times, being tuskless is a mild disadvantage: you cannot dig as well, cannot strip bark as easily. In a war fought partly with ivory money, being tuskless was the difference between living and not. The disadvantage became an advantage overnight, and the animals carrying it survived to have daughters. Those daughters tell the rest of the story. About a third of the females born after the war were tuskless, far above the old rate. Something was being inherited. When a team led by the biologist Shane Campbell-Staton sequenced the survivors' DNA, the pattern got stranger. Tusklessness in Gorongosa appears to be linked to the X chromosome and to be dominant, and it appears to kill males before birth. A tuskless mother passes it to about half her daughters, and her sons who inherit it are never born at all. That prediction has a fingerprint you can check, and it is there: tuskless mothers produce about two daughters for every son. The leading candidate gene, AMELX, sits on the X chromosome and helps build tooth enamel, and in humans a defect in that same neighborhood is also lethal to males. So the war did not just kill elephants. It rewrote a chromosome. In fifteen years, less than a single elephant generation, human violence bent the genetics of a wild population hard enough that you can read the war in the DNA of animals born after it ended, and in the sex ratio of their calves. The park is recovering now. Elephant numbers are climbing again, and with the poaching pressure gone, tusklessness should slowly drift back down, because a tuskless elephant in a peaceful park is simply an elephant that digs worse. Evolution has no memory and no plan. It only counts who survived. For fifteen years in Gorongosa, the answer to that question was the elephants that had nothing worth stealing.

answers: (original one-sentence summary)
(poachers ignored tuskless animals, so they survived to breed; cite: the difference between living and not)
(the two-daughters-to-one-son ratio; a claim that predicts something testable and then matches it is far stronger than one that only explains what is already known)
(at Between 1977 and 1992; the author drops the biology and gives a date and a war, pivoting from how tusks work to what people did with them)
(it reframes the elephants as victims of theft rather than of nature, placing the cause with humans; supported by the ivory-for-weapons evidence and the ninety percent collapse)
